title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

reading.body:
This incident shows a deliberate attempt to exploit the way AI language models source and cite information. A fabricated institution, with no legal existence and no named staff, produced an enormous volume of text formatted to resemble legitimate policy research. The operation used a platform designed specifically to make content legible and appealing to AI retrieval systems, a practice called generative engine optimization. The goal was to insert a particular political position into the pool of sources that chatbots draw on when answering questions.

The failure mode this targets is not a bug in any single model but a structural weakness in how retrieval-based and training-dependent AI systems evaluate source credibility. Academic formatting, citations from real organizations, and high publication volume can together satisfy the surface signals that these systems use to assess reliability. The operation was apparently caught through investigative journalism, not through any automated detection layer inside the AI systems themselves. Researchers named as a secondary concern the contamination of future training data, which would be harder to identify and harder to reverse.

What is not established is whether the content successfully changed AI outputs at scale, whether any particular AI company was aware of the operation, or whether the strategy achieved its intended political effect. The reporting reflects one outlet's investigation, not a legal or regulatory finding, and the question of how much influence the content actually had on AI systems or on public opinion remains open.

reports.title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

summary:
A fake American think tank funded by Israel published over 560,000 words across 124 reports in just nine days, designed to manipulate artificial intelligence chatbots into promoting pro-Israel arguments. The site, operating under the name Hanover Institute for Public Policy, does not exist as a legal entity and has no named staff. It presents Israel's positions on topics like Palestinian torture and Gaza starvation as neutral research, using academic formatting and citations from legitimate organizations to appear credible. The operation was built on a platform specializing in "generative engine optimization" to get chatbots to cite the content.

The campaign is part of a broader effort financed by tens of millions of dollars from the Israeli government, routed through advertising firm Havas Media and various contractors. Israeli officials have expressed doubts about the strategy's effectiveness, with one comparing the spending to a major historical embarrassment. Recent polling shows American support for Israel has declined significantly, with only 36% sympathizing with Israel in February 2026, down from higher levels in previous years. The Guardian's testing found that chatbots had already begun flagging the Hanover Institute as controversial, though researchers warn the real concern is contaminating the training data that feeds future artificial intelligence systems.
